meta.blurb: A Persian astronomer, a roadside inn, a jug of wine and a question nobody can answer. Omar Khayyam's four-line poems, and the English poet who made them famous, ask how to live well when life is short.
meta.bible: The Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam: a collection of rubaiyat, Persian four-line poems (quatrains), attributed to Omar Khayyam; scholars doubt that all of them are really his. Omar Khayyam: Persian mathematician, astronomer and poet, born in Nishapur about 1048, died about 1131; Khayyam means tent-maker. Nishapur: the city in Khorasan, in Persia (now Iran), where he was born and died. Balkh and Samarkand: cities where he studied and worked. Isfahan: the Persian capital where he led an observatory. Sultan Malik-Shah: the ruler who invited him to Isfahan about 1074. Nizam al-Mulk: the Sultan's chief minister. The Jalali calendar: the very accurate calendar made under Malik-Shah about 1079. Edward FitzGerald: English writer (1809 to 1883) from Suffolk who published a free English version in 1859; he rewrote it several times and a fifth edition came after his death in 1889. Edward Cowell: his friend and Persian teacher, who found a manuscript in an Oxford library. Bernard Quaritch: the London bookseller who published the first small edition in 1859, anonymously, with 75 quatrains. Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Algernon Swinburne: poets who praised it and made it known. Elihu Vedder: the American artist who illustrated an edition in 1884. Jamshyd: a legendary Persian king with a famous cup. Kaikobad: a legendary king. Bahram: a legendary Persian king and great hunter of the wild ass. Themes: the speed of time, the moving finger, the potter and the clay, the caravanserai (roadside inn), the book of verses, bread and wine, the sky like a bowl, the chessboard of days, the unanswered questions about heaven and hell. Whether the wine of the poems is real wine or a sign of love and spirit is argued by readers; the text says so and does not choose. Voice and tone: calm, curious, gently humorous and a little sad; respectful of every faith; careful to say 'attributed to' and 'the story says' where facts are uncertain; no invented dates.

beats.summary: The Rubaiyat is a collection of Persian four-line poems, attributed to Omar Khayyam and made famous in English.

beats.scene: A boy walks through the busy streets of a Persian city with domed roofs

beats.scene: Omar draws circles and curves on a sheet of paper, with a ruler in his hand
beats.summary: Omar writes an important book on algebra, showing how to solve cubic equations with geometry.

beats.scene: A great round building with a telescope-like tube on a hill, astronomers at work
beats.summary: Sultan Malik-Shah invites Omar to Isfahan, where he helps to lead a new observatory about 1074.

beats.scene: Scholars lean over a large table of tables and charts, a new calendar before them
beats.summary: About 1079 Omar and his colleagues make a new calendar, the Jalali calendar, which is very accurate.

beats.scene: A quiet scholar writes four lines of verse on a scrap of paper at night
beats.summary: Omar is known for four-line poems, but scholars doubt how many of the poems attributed to him are really his.

beats.scene: A cup lifted at dawn as the last stars fade over a garden
beats.summary: The best-known poem begins at dawn, with the stars driven away and a voice calling people to wake.

beats.scene: A moving finger of light writes on a dark wall while a man watches
beats.summary: The poet says that a moving finger writes, and nothing, not even tears or cleverness, can wash out a word.

beats.scene: Two doors, one marked yesterday and one marked tomorrow, with a person between them
beats.summary: A poem says two days need never trouble us: the day that has gone and the day that has not come.

beats.scene: A garden in spring with roses, a stream and a bird, and a golden cup on the grass
beats.summary: The poems praise spring, the rose and the garden, and the legendary cup of King Jamshyd.

beats.scene: A roadside inn with arched doorways and tired camels resting in the courtyard at dusk
beats.summary: The poet likens the world to a caravanserai, a roadside inn with two doors, night and day, where kings too must stay a short while.

beats.scene: A lion and a wild ass stand among broken pillars of a ruined royal hall
beats.summary: The poet imagines the halls of old kings now empty, and the great hunter Bahram sleeping while the wild ass walks over his grave.

beats.scene: A book, a jug, a loaf of bread and two people sitting in the shade of a tree
beats.summary: The poem imagines a happy picture: a book of verses under a tree, a jug of wine, a loaf of bread and a loved one nearby.

beats.scene: A jug and a Sufi's open hand beside a tavern doorway, the light behind them
beats.summary: Readers disagree whether the wine in the poems is real wine or a symbol of love and the spirit.

beats.scene: A traveller stands at a dark doorway in a rock wall, looking into the night
beats.summary: The poet says no one has ever come back from the other side to tell us the road, and so he turns from fear and hope.

beats.scene: A young man leaves a crowded lecture hall past a priest and a teacher
beats.summary: Omar, as a young man, listened to doctors and saints, and in the end he came out of the same door by which he went in.

beats.scene: A glowing small figure returns to a man on a hillside at night
beats.summary: In a famous poem the poet sends his soul out to ask about the next life, and the soul comes back to say that it is itself heaven and hell.

beats.scene: A locked door in a wall, and a veil hanging beside it, with no key anywhere
beats.summary: The poet says there is a door for which no key can be found and a veil that no one can see through.

beats.scene: A river flows on while a man stands on the bank, spreading his hands in wonder
beats.summary: The poet says that we come into the world without being asked, like flowing water, and leave it like the wind.

beats.scene: The night sky as an upturned bowl over a lonely man with his hands raised
beats.summary: The poet says not to lift hands to the sky for help, for the sky is as helpless as we are.

beats.scene: A giant chessboard of black and white squares with human figures as the pieces
beats.summary: The poet imagines the world as a chessboard of nights and days where destiny plays with people as pieces.

beats.scene: A polo ball rolls across a green field while a horseman chases it
beats.summary: The poet says that a ball in a game does not choose; it goes where the player strikes it, and so we go as fate drives us.

beats.scene: A potter's workshop with rows of clay pots and cups on shelves at dusk
beats.summary: One evening the poet stands alone in a potter's shop among the rows of clay pots.

beats.scene: Clay pots on a shelf seem to talk to each other, one tall and one small
beats.summary: In the poet's story, the pots ask who the potter is and who the pot; one says that the Maker is kind.

beats.scene: A clay cup tilted by a woman's hand over a bowl
beats.summary: Another pot says its clay has gone dry in the long years and begs to be filled with the old familiar drink.

beats.scene: A potter at his wheel, his hands wet with clay and a pot beneath them
beats.summary: The poet remembers a potter thumping wet clay that whispered to him, gently, brother, gently.

beats.scene: A single red rose growing in a green garden beside an old stone tomb
beats.summary: The poet says the rose is redder where a king is buried and each hyacinth may spring from a once-lovely head.

beats.scene: Dust blowing across an empty table where a cup and a book once stood
beats.summary: The poem says we shall turn to dust, and under the dust there will be no wine, no song, no singer, so make the most of the time left.

beats.scene: An angel figure carrying a jar on his shoulder approaches a tavern door at dusk
beats.summary: In one poem, the poet sees a shape like an angel at the tavern door, carrying a jar, and invites him to taste.

beats.scene: Two friends sit among ruins at night, reaching up toward a starry sky
beats.summary: The poet says that if he and his beloved could conspire with fate to seize the whole sorry scheme, they would shatter it and remake it nearer to the heart's desire.

beats.scene: A small bird flying quickly over a sandy path under a bright sky
beats.summary: The poet warns that the bird of time has only a little way to fly, and already it is on the wing.

beats.scene: Snow melting in a bright patch on a sand dune under the morning sun
beats.summary: The poem says that worldly hope turns to ashes or prospers, and soon, like snow on the desert, it vanishes.

beats.scene: A man waves away a distant drum and holds out a handful of coins
beats.summary: The poet says that some seek the glories of this world and some a future paradise, but he prefers the cash in hand to the sound of a drum far away.

beats.scene: A man in a long coat sits alone at a desk, reading and smiling slightly
beats.summary: Readers have seen Omar as a doubter, a mystic or a joker, and scholars do not agree.

beats.scene: A young Englishman reads at a desk in a country house in Suffolk with a Persian book
beats.summary: Edward FitzGerald, an English writer from Suffolk, learns Persian from a friend, Edward Cowell.

beats.summary: In 1859 the bookseller Bernard Quaritch publishes FitzGerald's version anonymously with 75 quatrains.

beats.scene: A box of unsold books marked with a low price outside a bookshop, a man stooping to look
beats.summary: The story says that unsold copies were put in a bargain box at a penny each, where poets found them.

beats.scene: Poets reading aloud in an armchair-filled room, a thin book passed from hand to hand
beats.summary: Poets such as Rossetti and Swinburne praise the poem, and it becomes very famous.

beats.scene: A writer crosses out lines and writes new ones, a Persian book open beside him
beats.summary: FitzGerald admits that his version is free: he joined, changed and rearranged the quatrains, and rewrote it again and again.

beats.scene: A single day shown in four panels: dawn, noon, evening and a starry night
beats.summary: FitzGerald gave the poem a shape like a single day, from dawn to evening to night, though the Persian poems have no such order.

beats.scene: A hand writing four short lines in a graceful curve with three ending the same way
beats.summary: A rubai has four lines, and the first, second and fourth usually end with the same sound.

beats.scene: Several different books of poems in different bindings lie on a long table
beats.summary: Later translators have given other versions of the poems, some plainer and more witty than FitzGerald's.

beats.scene: An illustrated page showing a figure with a cup, framed by flowers and moons
beats.summary: The poem has been illustrated, set to music and loved for generations; artists such as Elihu Vedder drew pictures for an 1884 edition.

beats.scene: An old man sits quietly beneath a tree in a Persian garden, the sun low
beats.summary: Omar dies about 1131 in Nishapur; a story says he wanted to be buried where the north wind would scatter blossoms over his grave.

beats.scene: A pale modern tomb with tall open arches in a garden in Nishapur
beats.summary: In 1963 a new tomb for Omar was built in Nishapur, in a garden, and people still visit it.

beats.scene: Omar at night looking through an instrument at the stars above a city
beats.summary: The scholar who measured the sky was also the poet who wondered about it; both come from the same curiosity.

beats.scene: A reader smiles over a small book on a park bench, a cup beside her
beats.summary: The poems are still read because they are short, honest and ask the questions that everyone asks.

beats.scene: Friends sharing a simple meal in a garden at sunset, laughing together
beats.summary: What readers take from the poems: be present, enjoy small things and be kind to each other, for time is short.

beats.scene: A guest rises from a table among stars scattered on grass and turns a cup over

B1B2: A rubai is a short Persian poem with four lines, and the plural is rubaiyat. These poems are attributed to Omar Khayyam, who lived about nine hundred years ago.
Omar was born about 1048 in Nishapur, a busy city in Persia, which is now Iran. His family name, Khayyam, means tent-maker, and some people think his family made tents.
Omar studied mathematics, astronomy and philosophy in Nishapur and in other great cities such as Balkh and Samarkand. He soon became known as one of the best scholars of his time.
Omar wrote a famous book on algebra, which is a way of solving problems with numbers and letters. In it he showed how to solve harder equations, called cubic equations, by drawing curves.
Sultan Malik-Shah, the ruler of the land, invited Omar to the city of Isfahan about 1074. There Omar and other scholars built an observatory to measure the movements of the stars.
About 1079 the scholars at the observatory made a new calendar, called the Jalali calendar. It measured the length of the year with great accuracy, and the modern Iranian calendar is based on it.
Omar is said to have written poems of four lines as well. However, many poems that carry his name were written by other people later, so no one is sure how many are really his.
In the English version, the famous poem begins at dawn. The night is over, the stars are fading, and a voice calls the sleepers to wake up and enjoy the day.
One famous poem says that a moving finger writes and then moves on. Neither goodness nor cleverness can call it back, and not all our tears can wash out a single word.
In some versions, a poem says that two days should never worry us. One is yesterday, which has gone, and the other is tomorrow, which has not been born.
The poems often return to the spring, when the garden is green and the roses open. They also speak of the seven-ringed cup of the old king Jamshyd, in which people said they could see the world.
The poet says that the world is like a caravanserai, a roadside inn for travellers. Night and day are its two doors, and even the greatest kings, such as Jamshyd, stay there only a short time.
The poem says that wild animals now walk where Jamshyd once feasted. Bahram, the great hunter, sleeps in his grave, and the wild ass he once hunted walks over his head.
One of the best-loved poems draws a simple picture. It shows a book of verses under a tree, a jug of wine, a loaf of bread, and a loved one singing beside the poet in the wild country.
Some readers think that the wine in the poems is real wine. Others believe that it is a symbol of love or of the spirit, and no one can prove which is right.

The poet says that countless people have gone through the door of darkness, and not one has returned to describe the road. For this reason he sets aside both the fear of hell and the hope of paradise.
The poet says that when he was young he listened eagerly to wise teachers and holy men. However, he heard great arguments and learned little, and he left by the same door through which he went in.
In a famous poem, the poet sends his soul out to learn about the life after death. By and by the soul returns and says that heaven and hell are inside every person.
The poet says that there was a door to which he found no key. There was also a veil through which he could not see, and no one could explain it.
The poet says that we come into this world without knowing why or from where, like water that flows. We leave it without knowing where we are going, like the wind that blows over the desert.
The poet calls the sky an upside-down bowl under which we live and die. He says that we should not lift our hands to it for help, because it is as helpless as we are.
The poet imagines the world as a chessboard of black nights and white days. Destiny plays with people as if they were pieces, moves them about, and puts them back in the box.
The poet says that a ball in a game of polo never asks yes or no. It goes wherever the player hits it, and he says that we are like that ball.
The poet tells a story. One evening, near the end of the fasting month, he was standing alone in an old potter's shop with rows of clay pots all around him.
In the poet's dream, the pots begin to talk, and one of them asks who the potter really is and who the pot is. Some of them say that the maker is unkind, but others say that he is good.
Another pot says with a long sigh that its clay has been dry for ages. It asks to be filled with the familiar wine, so that it may feel alive again.
In another verse the poet remembers watching a potter thump his wet clay. The clay seemed to whisper, gently, brother, gently, as if it had once been a living person.
The poet thinks that the rose may be brighter where an old king lies buried. Every flower in the garden, he says, may have grown from someone who was once alive and lovely.
The poet says that one day we will be dust, and under the dust there will be no song and no singer. So he urges us to make the most of the time we still have.
One poem tells how the poet saw an angel-like figure at the tavern door at dusk. The figure carried a jar on his shoulder and told the poet to taste what was inside.
In a bold verse, the poet says that if he and his love could take hold of fate, they would break the world into pieces. Then they would make it again, closer to what the heart wants.
The poet says that the bird of time has only a little way to fly. He adds that the bird is already in the air, so there is no time to waste.
The poem says that the hopes people have for money and power may turn to ashes or may succeed. Either way, they soon disappear, like snow that lies on the desert for a short hour.

Some people, says the poet, want the glories of this world, and others dream of paradise to come. For his part, he says, take what you can enjoy now, and do not mind the faint sound of a distant drum.
Readers have described Omar in many ways. Some see a doubter, some see a mystic who loved God, and some see a clever man who liked to joke, and scholars still disagree.
Edward FitzGerald was an English writer who lived quietly in Suffolk. He learned Persian from his friend Edward Cowell, who found a manuscript of the poems in an Oxford library.
In 1859 the bookseller Bernard Quaritch printed FitzGerald's version as a thin little book. It had seventy-five poems and no name on the cover, and at first almost nobody wanted it.
The story says that Quaritch could not sell the little book, so he put copies in a box outside his shop at a penny each. Some writers found them there and began to talk about them.
Poets such as Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Algernon Swinburne read it and praised it to their friends. Soon the book was famous, and more and more people wanted a copy.
FitzGerald admitted that his version was a free one. He changed lines, joined some poems together and moved others about, and he rewrote the book several times during his life.
FitzGerald arranged the poems so that they seem to follow one day, from morning to night. The Persian original has no such order, because it is just a collection of separate quatrains.
A rubai is a short poem of four lines. In Persian, the first, second and fourth lines usually end with the same sound, so the poem feels complete and neat.
After FitzGerald, many other writers have made new versions of the poems in English and in other languages. Some are plainer than his, and some are closer to the Persian.
Many artists have drawn pictures for the poem, and musicians have set it to music. In 1884 an American artist, Elihu Vedder, made a famous book of pictures for it.
Omar died in his home city of Nishapur about 1131, when he was old. A story says he asked to be buried in a place where the wind would scatter blossoms on his grave.
In 1963 a handsome new tomb was built for Omar in a garden in Nishapur. Visitors from Iran and from all over the world still come to see it.
The man who measured the stars was also the man who wondered about them in poems. Both kinds of work came from the same wish to understand the world.
People still read these poems because they are short and clear, and they ask questions that everybody asks. They do not claim to know all the answers.
Many readers take the same message from the poems. Time is short, so enjoy small things today, be kind to the people near you and do not waste the day on worry.
In FitzGerald's last verse, the poet speaks to his beloved. When she walks among the guests in the garden and reaches the place where he sat, she should turn down an empty glass.
C1C2: The Rubaiyat is a collection of rubaiyat, the Persian name for short poems of four lines, which are attributed to Omar Khayyam, a scholar who lived nearly nine centuries ago. They became famous around the world through an English version published in 1859, and since then they have been loved, argued over and quoted by millions of readers. Few books so small have travelled so far.

Omar was born about 1048 in Nishapur, a prosperous and learned city in the Persian province of Khorasan, in what is now north-eastern Iran. His family name, Khayyam, means tent-maker, and it may have come from his father's trade, though nobody can say for certain. The city was famous for its schools, its libraries and its busy bazaars.

As a young man Omar studied mathematics, astronomy and philosophy, first in Nishapur and then in other great centres of learning such as Balkh and Samarkand. He had an unusually quick and curious mind, and his reputation as a scholar spread long before he reached middle age. People who knew him said that he forgot nothing that he had once read.

While working in Samarkand, Omar wrote a famous book on algebra, in which he set out how to solve cubic equations, the difficult problems that contain a number multiplied by itself three times. He did it not with a simple formula but with geometry, finding the answer where two carefully drawn curves cross. Historians of mathematics still admire the clarity of his method.

About 1074 the ruler of the land, Sultan Malik-Shah, invited Omar to the capital city of Isfahan, where he and his chief minister, Nizam al-Mulk, planned a great observatory. Omar became one of its leading astronomers, charting the slow movements of the heavens night after night, and he would remember the patience that this work required for the rest of his life. It was among the finest scientific posts of his age.

Around the year 1079, the astronomers at Isfahan completed a new calendar named the Jalali calendar, after the Sultan, who had commissioned it to keep the farming and tax seasons in step with the sun. It measured the length of the year with remarkable accuracy, and the calendar still used in Iran today descends from it. The work was a triumph of careful observation.

Omar is said to have scribbled poems of four lines in his spare moments, but the evidence is thin, and many verses that carry his name were added by later writers. Scholars still argue about how many of the rubaiyat are really his, and some believe that only a small number can be proved to be genuine. Fortunately, the poems can be enjoyed without settling the question.

The best-known English version opens at dawn, with the stars scattered out of the sky by the rising sun, and a voice calling the sleepers outside a tavern to wake and fill the cup before life runs dry. The mood is cheerful yet urgent, for the speaker knows that the morning will not wait for anybody. It is a call to be awake to the day.

One of the best-loved poems says that a moving finger writes and, having written, moves on, and that neither piety nor wit can lure it back to cancel half a line. Not all our tears, it adds, can wash out a single word of what has been done. The image makes the past feel as fixed as ink, and it reminds the reader that today, too, is being written.

In some versions, a poem observes that there are two days on which we need never worry: the day that has died and cannot be recalled, and the day that has not yet been born and cannot be known. Between those two lies only the day we are living in, the one that truly belongs to us. It is advice that readers in every century have found easy to admire and hard to follow.

Again and again the poems return to spring, when the earth turns green, the rose unfolds, and the birds sing in the garden. They also remember the legendary cup of King Jamshyd, a seven-ringed vessel in which, according to the old Persian stories, the whole world could be seen. The reader is invited to look at the real garden instead of searching for a magical one.

To the poet, the world is a battered caravanserai, one of those roadside inns where merchants and their camels rest for a night, and its two doorways are Night and Day. Great kings such as Jamshyd and Kaikobad once feasted in it, he notes, and now they are gone, their places filled by other travellers who also will not stay. We are all guests here, he suggests, and should behave with grace.

The poet pictures the courts where Jamshyd once gloried and drank deep, and says that the lion and the lizard keep them now. Bahram, the great hunter of the wild ass, lies asleep in his grave while the creature he once chased tramples over his head and cannot disturb his rest. The lesson, offered without anger, is that power is a short loan.

One of the most celebrated poems paints a picture so simple that it has become a symbol of quiet happiness: a book of verses beneath the branches, a flask of wine, a loaf of bread, and a beloved companion singing nearby in the wilderness. The wilderness, the poet adds, would then be paradise enough. It is a vision of contentment that requires neither wealth nor a palace.

Wine is everywhere in the poems, and readers have never agreed about what it means: some take it literally, as a call to enjoy the pleasures of life, while others see a symbol of love, joy or the spirit, as in much Persian mystical poetry. Both readings have been defended with learning and passion, and the text itself gives no final answer. Perhaps the poet intended to leave the question open.

Of the millions who have passed through the door of darkness before us, the poet remarks, not one has returned to describe the road, and so nobody really knows what lies beyond it. He therefore sets aside both the threat of hell and the promise of paradise, and turns his attention to the one thing that is certain, that this life is flying past. Some readers hear scepticism in this, and others hear honest humility.

In one verse, the poet recalls that in his youth he eagerly sought out the doctors and the saints and listened to their great arguments about life and the world. When it was all over, he says with a rueful smile, he walked out through the very same door by which he had come in, no wiser than before. The verse has comforted many people who have studied hard and still wondered.

In a much-loved poem, the speaker sends his soul into the Invisible to spell out some letter from the life to come, and after a while the soul comes back and answers that it is itself both heaven and hell. The verse can be understood as a hint that joy and sorrow are found within the heart rather than far away. It is one of several places where the poem turns from doubt to a kind of wisdom.

There was a door, says the poet, to which he could find no key, and there was a veil through which he could not see, however hard he tried. For a little while, he adds, people talk of you and me, and then they stop, and the veil falls again. The mystery of existence is a locked room that every thinking person must stand in front of.

We came into the universe, says the poet, without knowing why or whence, like water flowing wherever the land leads it, and we go out of it like wind blowing across the desert, not knowing where we are bound. The picture is not bitter but strangely peaceful, since it suggests that nobody has been given an examination without having been given the answers. We are travellers, not judges.

The poet likens the heavens to an overturned bowl beneath which we all live and die, and he advises us not to lift our hands to it in search of an answer, for it rolls on as helplessly as you or I. Such a thought might seem bleak, but it carries a kind of freedom: we are not at the mercy of the stars. The poet, after all, spent his working life measuring them.

In another image, the world is a chessboard of nights and days on which Destiny plays with men for pieces, moving them hither and thither, checkmating some and capturing others, and then laying them one by one back in the box. The picture is a little humorous and a little grim, and it makes the poet's advice sound all the more sensible. If life is a game, he implies, we may as well enjoy the moves.

A ball on the polo field, the poet says, makes no argument of yes or no, but goes wherever the player's stick sends it, and so, he suggests, do human beings. The one who has thrown us into the field alone knows why, and he alone knows where. It is a bold and somewhat daring thought, and the poem expresses it with perfect calm.

In one of the best-known sections, the poet describes how he once stood alone at dusk in an old potter's shop, near the close of the month of fasting, with the clay population round him in neat rows. The shop was quiet, the light was fading, and the pots stood on their shelves like a silent audience waiting for somebody to begin. Then, to his surprise, the vessels began to speak.

The pots, in the poet's fancy, begin to talk among themselves, and a loud-lipped vessel asks who the potter is, and who the pot. Another says that it has heard of a maker who threatens to throw the luckless pots he spoiled into hell, but it adds with a shrug that he is a good fellow, and all will be well. The conversation is funny and bold, and it mixes laughter with a serious thought.

A third pot sighs and remarks that its clay has gone dry through long oblivion, and it begs to be filled with the old familiar juice so that it may recover by and by. Another observes that it was surely not made in vain, only to be broken and trampled back into earth. In the end the pots find comfort not in answers but in each other, which is perhaps the point.

In another verse the poet remembers stopping by the way to watch a potter pressing and thumping his wet clay, and imagines that the clay murmured to its maker, Gently, brother, gently, pray. The thought behind it is that the clay of the pots may once have been a human being, and deserves tenderness. The image has made many readers look at an ordinary cup with new respect.

The poet wonders whether the rose ever blows so red as where some buried king lies, and whether every hyacinth in the garden may have dropped into her lap from some once lovely head. It is a gentle, strangely beautiful thought, the idea that the earth is made of those who came before us, and that the spring is their reply. The grave and the garden turn out to be one place.

Before we too descend into the dust, says the poet, let us make the most of what we may yet spend, for dust lying under dust has neither wine nor song nor singer, and not even an end to look forward to. The verse is blunt, yet its purpose is not to frighten but to wake the reader up. It sounds almost like an alarm bell in the middle of a very pleasant afternoon.

One poem describes how, lately, an angel shape came stealing through the dusk to the tavern door, bearing a vessel on his shoulder, and bade the poet taste what was inside. The scene belongs to the dream world of the poems, where tavern and holy place seem to mingle. A literal reader sees a jar of wine, and a mystical reader sees a gift from heaven.

In one of the boldest verses, the speaker turns to his beloved and says that, if the two of them could conspire with fate to seize this sorry scheme of things entire, they would shatter it to bits and then remould it nearer to the heart's desire. It is the cry of anyone who has looked at the world's suffering and wished that it were kinder. The poem does not pretend that the wish can come true.

The bird of Time, says the poet, has but a little way to flutter, and look, the bird is already on the wing, so there is no leisure to waste on grudges, regrets or empty ambition. The image is quick and unforgettable, for we all feel the years passing faster than we expected. It makes the garden, the cup and the friend sitting beside us seem all the more precious.

The worldly hope on which men set their hearts, the poet remarks, turns to ashes or prospers, and soon afterwards, like snow on the dusty face of the desert, it shines for an hour or two and is gone. He does not despise success, but he refuses to be dazzled by it. It is a modest, sober thought, all the more striking for the glittering world in which he lived.

Some people, says the poet, long for the glories of this world, while others sigh for the paradise to come, but for his part he would rather take the cash in hand and let the credit go. The brave music of a distant drum, he adds, sounds fine from afar and does little for the person beside you. It is a joke at the expense of both the greedy and the over-promised.

Over the centuries Omar has been described as a sceptic who doubted everything, as a Sufi mystic whose wine stood for divine love, and as a clever man who simply liked to tease the pious and the proud. Scholars still disagree, partly because so few of the poems can be shown to be his, and partly because the poems themselves are so open-handed. Each reader, perhaps, finds the Omar he or she needs.

Edward FitzGerald, born in 1809, was a shy and unambitious English gentleman who lived much of his life quietly in the county of Suffolk, reading and writing for his own pleasure. His friend Edward Cowell, who taught him Persian, discovered an old manuscript of the quatrains in an Oxford library and sent him a copy. FitzGerald took it up, and the poems took hold of him.

In 1859 the London bookseller Bernard Quaritch published FitzGerald's version as a thin pamphlet containing seventy-five quatrains, and the translator, who was never comfortable with publicity, did not put his name to it. Almost nobody noticed. The book was a quiet failure, and for a time it seemed that these poems, which had survived for centuries in Persia, would be forgotten in England within a few months.

The story says that when the copies would not sell, the bookseller placed them in a cheap box outside his shop, priced at a penny, where a few readers chanced to pick them up. Some of those readers were poets, and they were astonished by what they found. Whether the details are exactly true or have grown with the retelling, the little book was soon discovered.

Poets such as Dante Gabriel Rossetti and Algernon Swinburne read the little book with delight, and they praised it so loudly to their friends that by the 1860s it had begun to find a wide public. New editions were called for, and FitzGerald, who could hardly believe it, kept polishing the verses. By the end of the century the Rubaiyat was one of the most quoted poems in the English language.

FitzGerald never pretended that his work was a literal translation, and he cheerfully admitted that he had joined some quatrains together, changed others, and moved them about to suit the music of his English. He rewrote the whole book several times during his lifetime, and a fifth edition appeared after his death in 1883. In a sense, he made a new poem, with Omar as its distant parent.

FitzGerald arranged the verses so that the whole poem feels like a single day, opening at dawn, moving through the heat of noon and the thoughts of the afternoon, and closing in the darkness of night. The Persian original has no such order, since it is simply a collection of separate quatrains that could be read in any sequence. The pleasing shape was the English poet's gift.

In Persian, a rubai is built on a strict and satisfying pattern: four lines, of which the first, second and fourth usually end on the same rhyme, while the third is free. This neat design leaves room for a small turn of thought, so that the last line lands like a final note. It suits Omar's style perfectly, because a very short poem can hold a very large doubt.

After FitzGerald, many other translators made new versions of the quatrains, in English and in dozens of other languages, and some of them tried to stay closer to the Persian. Their Omar is often plainer, more concrete and more wryly funny than FitzGerald's, and the differences between the versions show how much a translation is an act of interpretation. A reader who enjoys one version may well enjoy comparing several.

Few poems have inspired so many other kinds of art: composers have set the verses to music, and painters and printers have decorated them with moons, flowers and winged figures. In 1884 the American artist Elihu Vedder produced a famous illustrated edition that made the poem a favourite among readers who loved handsome books. Clubs of admirers even met to read the quatrains aloud over a cup.

Omar died at Nishapur about 1131, an old man, after a career that had taken him from the schools of Khorasan to the courts of Isfahan and back again. A story told by a later visitor says that he wished to be buried in a spot where the north wind would scatter blossoms over his grave. Years afterwards, the story adds, the visitor found the tomb covered in fallen petals.

A handsome mausoleum with tall, slender arches was built for him in a garden at Nishapur in 1963, designed by the Iranian architect Hooshang Seyhoun, and it has become a place of pilgrimage for lovers of poetry. Visitors from Iran and from many other countries come to stand beside his grave, some of them carrying a book. It is perhaps the best tribute that the quiet scholar could have wished for.

Omar the astronomer, who spent whole nights measuring the slow movements of the heavens, and Omar the poet, who wondered what the whole thing meant, may be one man with a single, tireless curiosity. The scientist wants exact answers, and the poet accepts that some questions have none, and between them they make a fuller picture of what it is to be human. If the verses are his, they are an astronomer's honest shrug.

These poems are still read today because they are short, vivid and honest, and because they ask the questions that every thoughtful person eventually asks about time, death and the point of it all. They do not claim to know the answers, and they never preach, which is a rare quality in poems about such large matters. A reader may leave them with a smile instead of a lecture.

Readers have taken many different lessons from the Rubaiyat, but the commonest is the simplest: time is short, so make the most of today, delight in small things, and be good to the people who sit beside you. This is not a rule of the poems so much as a feeling that rises from them, as warm as a lamp in a dark room. The poet's thoughts may be sad, but his advice is kind.

In the closing verse of FitzGerald's version, the speaker imagines his beloved walking, with a shining foot, among the guests scattered like stars on the grass, and on her joyous errand reaching the spot where he once sat. There, he asks, she should turn down an empty glass in his memory. It is a tender and quietly brave ending, and it leaves the reader in the garden at dusk, thinking of absent friends.
